m: Antibiotics help viral upper respiratory infections by preventing secondary infection.
fix: Routine antibiotics do not prevent complications in viral URTI and drive resistance and side effects.

m: Resistance develops because the patient's body becomes used to the antibiotic.
fix: Bacteria, not patients, become resistant through selection and gene transfer driven by antibiotic exposure.

m: Broader-spectrum antibiotics are always safer.
fix: Use the narrowest effective agent; de-escalate once culture results are known.

m: Isoniazid-related neuropathy is prevented by vitamin B12.
fix: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) prevents isoniazid peripheral neuropathy.

m: Heparin and warfarin are monitored with the same test.
fix: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with aPTT; warfarin with PT/INR.

m: Aspirin works by dissolving existing clots.
fix: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 to prevent new clot formation; fibrinolytics dissolve clots.

m: Thrombolysis is useful at any time after a stroke.
fix: Benefit is strictly time-dependent within a narrow window, and haemorrhage must be excluded first.

m: Loop and thiazide diuretics have the same effect on calcium.
fix: Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion; thiazides reduce it.

m: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should be combined for extra kidney protection.
fix: Dual blockade increases hyperkalaemia and kidney injury without added benefit.

m: Beta-blockers are first-line for all hypertension.
fix: First-line choice depends on age, ethnicity and comorbidity; beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.

m: Digoxin improves survival in heart failure.
fix: Digoxin reduces symptoms and admissions but not mortality; ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors improve survival.

m: Metformin commonly causes hypoglycaemia.
fix: Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycaemia; sulfonylureas and insulin do.

m: Inhaled steroids give quick relief in an asthma attack.
fix: Inhaled steroids control inflammation over time; short-acting beta-agonists give quick relief.

m: A short-acting reliever alone is adequate long-term treatment for persistent asthma.
fix: Persistent asthma needs inhaled corticosteroid-based controller therapy.

m: Patients with cancer pain on opioids quickly become addicted.
fix: Addiction is uncommon when opioids are used appropriately for cancer pain; tolerance and dependence are different from addiction.

m: Paracetamol is safe in any dose because it is available over the counter.
fix: Overdose causes hepatotoxicity; N-acetylcysteine is the antidote.

m: Doubling the dose doubles the duration of drug action.
fix: With first-order kinetics, doubling the dose prolongs action by about one half-life only.

m: Enzyme inducers increase the effect of drugs metabolised by that enzyme.
fix: Inducers speed metabolism and reduce effect (e.g. rifampicin with oral contraceptives); inhibitors increase it.

m: Most drugs are safe in pregnancy if they are safe in adults.
fix: Teratogenicity and altered pharmacokinetics mean drugs need specific pregnancy safety data.

m: Valproate is the preferred antiseizure medicine in women of childbearing age.
fix: Valproate is highly teratogenic; avoid it in women who may become pregnant unless no alternative exists.

m: Atypical antipsychotics have no important side effects.
fix: They cause weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia; metabolic monitoring is needed.

m: Antidepressants work fully within the first few days.
fix: Mood benefit usually takes 2–6 weeks; side effects appear earlier.

m: Live vaccines are safe in all immunocompromised patients.
fix: Live vaccines are generally contraindicated in significant immunosuppression and pregnancy.

m: An adverse drug reaction means the drug was given incorrectly.
fix: ADRs can occur with correct use at normal doses; they should still be reported to pharmacovigilance.

m: Gram-positive bacteria stain pink.
fix: Gram-positive organisms retain crystal violet and stain purple; Gram-negative ones stain pink with the counterstain.

m: Ziehl-Neelsen stain is used for all bacteria.
fix: It detects acid-fast organisms such as mycobacteria, which resist decolourisation with acid-alcohol.

m: Blood cultures can be taken after starting antibiotics without loss of yield.
fix: Antibiotics reduce culture yield; take cultures before the first dose whenever possible.

m: Disinfection and sterilisation mean the same thing.
fix: Sterilisation kills all microbes including spores; disinfection reduces pathogens but may not kill spores.

m: Wearing gloves removes the need for hand hygiene.
fix: Hand hygiene is needed before and after glove use; gloves can be contaminated or have micro-defects.

m: Herd immunity protects everyone once a few people are vaccinated.
fix: Herd immunity requires coverage above a threshold that depends on the disease's transmissibility.

m: Bacteria in the urine always need antibiotics.
fix: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is usually not treated, except in pregnancy and before urological procedures.

m: A urea breath test is reliable while the patient is on proton pump inhibitors.
fix: PPIs and recent antibiotics cause false negatives; stop them before testing.

m: Opportunistic infections occur only in HIV infection.
fix: They occur in any significant immunosuppression, including chemotherapy, transplantation and long-term steroids.

m: A negative HIV antibody test soon after exposure excludes infection.
fix: Tests can be negative in the window period; repeat testing is needed after exposure.

m: A positive IgG antibody indicates current infection.
fix: IgM suggests recent infection; IgG usually indicates past infection or immunity unless titres rise.

m: All bloody diarrhoea is amoebic.
fix: Shigella is the commonest cause of bloody diarrhoea in children; stool examination guides treatment.

m: Hookworm infection spreads mainly through contaminated food.
fix: Larvae penetrate the skin, usually through bare feet on contaminated soil.

m: Filariasis is spread by Anopheles mosquitoes only in India.
fix: In India, Culex quinquefasciatus is the main vector of Wuchereria bancrofti.

m: Encephalitis and meningitis present identically.
fix: Encephalitis causes altered behaviour, consciousness and seizures early; meningitis is dominated by meningeal signs.

m: Any fever without an obvious source is a PUO.
fix: PUO requires prolonged fever (classically >3 weeks) undiagnosed despite a defined period of investigation.
